paper_title: SynthFaces: Balanced Large Scale Human Dataset

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: The pursuit of fair and equitable AI in human-centric tasks is critically hindered by the inherent biases and privacy risks of real-world datasets, which offer imbalanced representations of identity and often contain sensitive personal information. Consequently, state-of-the-art generative models trained on this skewed data exhibit unfair performance, particularly in identity-preserving generation. In this work we propose a pipeline for controllable generation of dataset with diverse faces for generative models training and finetuning. We achieve this by expanding foundational Arc2Face diffusion model with a flow matching generative model in the manifold of identity embeddings. We demonstrate that such approach achieves both goals of generative fidelity and label diversity not present in real human-centric datasets. As a result we collect and further contextualize a highly balanced identity-centric dataset of humans named SynthFaces. By design, our released images and identities are synthetic, reducing direct reliance on real personal images; we empirically check identity separation with a nearest-neighbor non-leakage metric. We purpose it for training and tuning of fair models for various downstream tasks, and showcase its usability in finetuning an existing adapter-based method for personalized generation.

SynthFaces dataset collection pipeline is designed to address set of three core problems. 1) Label bias of existing datasets: both existing datasets with human faces, such as FFHQ, SHHQ [4], EasyPortrait [15] and CosmicMan-HQ [19] and generative samplers exhibit severe category imbalance - both unconditional samplers such as StyleGAN [25], as well as by conditional samplers e.g., Arc2Face [26], PhotoMaker [21] produce or reflect skewed distributions over demographic attributes (age, race, gender). 2) Face-similarity quality of conditional samplers: when evaluated per demographic group, conditional personalization models show uneven face preservation quality, which is natural given first problem; 3) Usage of real people identities: existing real datasets, especially large-scale ones, may include identities that did not give consent for deep learning model training or may include identities from under-age groups, using which may be completely unethical and certain datasets have been revoked from public access for that reason [7, 13]. Additionally, we aim to fulfill properties that are largely required for modern humancentric datasets - such properties are mentioned in Table 1, specifically we aim to provide Captions for images, describing both humans and surrounding context, collected images are ID-grouped, meaning that there are multiple images with same person, and lastly we aim to obtain HQ image with high resolution. These properties may be missing for certain types of datasets mentioned in table. For example under Raw Images we denote large-scale raw collections obtained via web-scrapping, are large enough to include all types of faces, however they might still require label-balancing strategy, as well image filtering to obtain high-quality images. HQ Captioned datasets are high quality, but they balance in human representation as we show later, as well as typically do not include multiple images of same person. Face Recognition datasets are typically also without captions, low resolution and also skewed in terms of human representation. In comparison our collected dataset satisfies all of these properties, while also using released images and identities that are synthetic and empirically screened for identity separation. Table 1: High level comparison of dataset types, in columns Caption denotes that images are paired with prompts, Balanced labels that dataset is balanced over selected demographic labels, ID-grouped that multiple images per person are provided and HQ suggests that images are high resolution and visually high quality

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.content: 3 Synthetic face datasets have been studied primarily for face recognition [1, 14, 18]. Existing pipelines combine GAN samples with per-identity adaptation [15, 29], or exploit the conditional space of face foundation models such as Arc2Face [26]. HyperFace [30] explores this hyperspherical space directly, but its generated identities remain demographically imbalanced. Arc2Face and Vec2Face [34] instead perturb real ArcFace embeddings with PCA, requiring real identity embeddings at inference time and offering no explicit separation from them. ID-Flow learns controllable prior over the identity manifold, samples without reference embeddings at inference time, and evaluates separation using ID-NonLeak  (Table 2)  . Model fairness seeks to reduce systematic performance differences across demographic subgroups [20, 24]. Our approach intervenes at data construction time by controlling the demographic distribution of sampled identities. Figure 1: Distribution of labels across different categories in some of conventional datasets with humans. Dashed lines denotes mean value across labels, color highlights values above mean Identity-preserving generation Identity-preserving generation conditions image synthesis on reference face. Introduced with adapter-based methods - IP-Adapter-FaceID [36], PhotoMaker [21], PuLID [8], and InstantID [32]; InfiniteYou [11] further improves fidelity and flexibility. Recent in-context models such as Qwen-Image [33] and Flux-2 [17] can preserve identity across varied contexts, whereas per-subject methods such as DreamBooth [29] require fine-tuning for every new identity. We use these models for contextualization after independently controlling the identity distribution.

sections.title: 3.1 Existing datasets biases
sections.content: To quantify label bias in existing datasets, we annotate them with FairFace classifier [12] and in Figure 1 show that all of the presented datasets demonstrate heavy bias towards certain 4 KARPUKHIN ET AL.: SYNTHFACES labels. Training on such data without empirical balancing strategies can be harmful for generative model fairness and diversity.

sections.title: 3.2 Evaluating unfairness in human-centric models
sections.content: To expose subgroup differences hidden by aggregate metrics, we construct FairBench, probe set sampled uniformly over FairFace label combinations. Figure 15 shows substantial demographic variation in identity preservation, consistent with the dataset skew in Figure 1. Section 5 evaluates whether balanced training data also improves subgroup parity in face recognition and demographic VQA.

sections.title: 4 Dataset construction
sections.content: In order to build dataset of synthetic released identities and images, we follow 3 stage design described in Figure 2. Each stage is motivated by specific problem of existing pipelines - at stage 1 we ensure that dataset is private while also free of skewed label distribution, at stage 2 we construct maximum fidelity faces from diverse identity representation, and at stage 3 we achieve high resolution and context coupled with captions.

sections.title: 4.1 Learning to sample identities
sections.content: Identity embeddings lie on unit hypersphere, so treating them as unconstrained Euclidean vectors ignores their geometry. We instead learn geodesic flow-matching model directly on this manifold. Figure 2: Dataset multi-stage collection pipeline. We aim to train generative model in latent space of identity embeddings. Natural observation is that these embeddings are all unit length and therefore exists on n-dimensional sphere. Some prior works tried to explore this idea, for example in [30] authors pose problem of sampling diverse embeddings as optimization problem on sphere, and in [3] authors construct von MisesFisher based diffusion model that respects manifold geometry. In this work we make novel adaptation of non-Euclidean flow matching to construct generative i=1 Sn, where ei = 1 for i, we aim to train vθ () model on identity latents. These projection are explicitly defined for known manifolds such as sphere, which allows to obtain training target without requiring simulation [22]. These labels are obtained through training data annotation and represent general face features, such as race, age and gender. During inference we use these to construct diverse dataset by applying classifier-free guidance [9]. We stick with simple multilayer MLP architecture with skipconnections and apply guidance scale 2.0 during sampling of identities. These embeddings as noted by Stage 2 plan, are turned into face images, and various filtering strategies are applied in order to enhance output of this stage and get rid of potential artifacts present in images. Image statistics filtering we start by analyzing distribution of images characteristics generated by Arc2Face. We evaluate conventional computer vision characteristics of images, such as entropy and saturation. We observe that tail of entropy distribution corresponds to heavily stylized images, low saturation values correspond to black and white images, and high saturation mostly coincides with faces that have unnatural amount of color/light or make up. Therefore we drop around p% of images from tails, removing approximately 3k unsatisfactory images. Qualitative examples are provided in supplementary Figure 11. Figure 6: Data filtering pipeline from Stage 2 to contextualization - in order to minimize amount of corrupted images with faces we 1) remove images in long tails of statistics 2) detect images with artifacts via vision-language model 3) threshold pairwise similarity, ensuring variability of identities in all categories, resulting in the end with approximately 150,000 final images 8 KARPUKHIN ET AL.: SYNTHFACES

sections.title: 4.2 Data curation pipeline
sections.content: VLM filtering After basic image statistics filtering we utilize multiple Qwen-VL models to assess obtained images from two perspectives 1) does the persons face align with labels that were used to generate them 2) does the persons face contain any visual artifacts. Based of VLM answers we drop all misaligned images and images that contained faces with visual defects, keeping samples which by majority voting of VLMs are assessed as well-aligned. To make sure that only relevant artifacts are dropped, we prompted VLM to reason about noticed artifacts in the images and dropped images only if the reasoning contained specific key-words. Detailed example of VLM prompting is provided in Appendix A.5. Comparison of metrics before and after filtering Stage 2 images. sections.content: Table 6: Comparison of HQ dataset metrics with SynthFaces - our dataset offers superior quality over Cosmic-HQ, while allowing richer contextualization without overly large faces Caption and label matching In order to contextualize images, we collected captions of images from real world datasets like Cosmic-HQ and FFHQ-in-the-Wild and collections of human related texts like HumanCaption [2]. We filtered prompts to exclude any details related to attributes that were controlled during identity sampling, including details with description of facial features. After that we roughly annotated these captions into subgroups based of their context, main factor being suitable age, e.g. prompts for child, prompts for adults, etc. After that we randomly sampled captions for each image given its label, matching label with classes with captions that are suitable for these face label values by looking for specific keywords that were used as person descriptors. In order to enhance realism of images generated with InfiniteYou we attach additional LoRAs for realism and deblurring, and to speed up generation with Flux 2 we utilize Turbo checkpoint that from experiments turned to be the best amongst existing models for personalized generation of humans, see qualitative comparison in Appendix A.7. As result, we obtain large scale, high quality diverse dataset of synthetic released identities, consisting in total of 150,000 captioned high-resolution images of varying aspect ratios, with approximately 10 images per identity. Resulting samples from this dataset are given in Fig. 7. Additionally, we evaluate resulting SynthFaces images in terms of image quality by ImageReward(IR) metric [35], text alignment by CLIP and ratio of size of face detection box to size of the image side. Compared with the baselines in Table 6, SynthFaces improves over Cosmic-HQ on ImageReward and CLIP while keeping faces smaller than FluxSynID, whose document-formatted images often lack background context.

sections.title: 5 Downstream applications
sections.content: We evaluate whether SynthFaces data yields fairness benefits in distinct downstream tasks: finetuning personalized generation pipeline, face recognition (FR) verification and demographic attribute classification. Fine-tuning tests usefulness for id-preserving generation, FR tests whether balanced synthetic identities reduce verification disparity, and VQA tests whether balanced human images help demographic attribute recognition. 5.1 ID-preserving generation Metrics We measure two core metrics for face preservation on average to observe mean change after adapter tuning, as well as per category analysis - ID - stands for face similarity between source and generated person, CLIP-T - measures similarity between image and prompt description in latent space of CLIP model. Figure 8: Face similarity measured across different categories of IpAdapter-FaceID before and after tuning on data generated by ID-flow. Evaluation We use two evaluation benchmarks - one is FairBench introduced before - which is collection of balanced faces that includes every possible combinations of labels, KARPUKHIN ET AL.: SYNTHFACES 11 its textual captions focus only on face description. This benchmark corresponds of to maximum reconstruction of person facial features. Second benchmark named Context is less diverse in terms of labels, but includes richer prompts specializing in placing people in contexts, demonstrating trade-off between face similarity being lower for smaller faces and more contextualized humans. Table 7: Effect of tuning pipelines with our dataset, reporting average metric values

sections.content: ID CLIP-T ID CLIP-T SD-1.5 + FaceID SD-1.5 + FaceID (+ tuned) 68.63 71. 32.91 33.27 28.81 28.49 53.56 51.56 Training details Finetuning conditional diffusion model comes with challenge of data distribution drift. Its problem that arises because of discrepancy between data that was used for training original checkpoint and data that is being used for finetuning. Main characteristic that seemingly may hurt performance of these methods in terms of face preservation is learned face size. Face size in collected data serves as hidden factor that can be learned by diffusion model and directly affect similarity metric. Therefore to mitigate effect of this hidden factor we apply approach from [5] termed shortcut finetuning - specifically we attach frozen ControlNet [37] to condition on human pose and face position in source image, making finetuned IP-adapter layers learn only essential features related to face preservation. Details about this approach and hyperparameters for training are given in Appendix A.8. We provide finetuning results for StableDiffusion coupled with IPAdapter-FaceID. We observe significant mean improvement in fair face reconstruction benchmark, while keeping comparable performance of contextualized generation. However, it is also important to inspect the change in quality per label. In Fig. 8 we showcase improvement across different label values per age and race groups - improvement is not isolated and ultimately makes performance more uniform. More detailed finetuning results with another personalized generation method are provided in Appendix A.8.

sections.title: 5.2 Face Recognition Fairness
sections.content: Setup We train FR model on version of our synthetic dataset purposed for this task - we sample 500k images from ID-Flow + Arc2Face with uniform labels, 50 images per identity, and additionally filter identities by similarity threshold in every subgroup. We compare with two other available FR model baselines: SynthFaces-500K (IResNet-100, ArcFace, 500K images of 10K identities from our pipeline), Vec2Face [34] (IResNet-50 SE, ArcFace, 300K images, HSFace300K real-web source), and HyperFace [30]. We evaluate on two regimes: (a) five standard FR benchmarks (LFW, CFP-FP, AgeDB-30, CALFW, CPLFW) annotated post-hoc with FairFace [12] demographic labels, and (b) BFW (Balanced Faces in the Wild) [27], balanced dataset with over 900K images balanced across 4 races 2 genders with human-assigned labels. Fairness metrics We aim to evaluate fairness of trained FR models. After analyzing standard FR benchmarks we find them to be heavily skewed (AgeDB-30: 88% White; LFW: 66% White, 75% male - see Table 14 in the Appendix), making accuracy-disparity metrics 12 KARPUKHIN ET AL.: SYNTHFACES conflate representation with bias. face verification system accepts or rejects pair against threshold τ; the two governing error rates are the False Match Rate (FMR) and False Non-Match Rate (FNMR) [6]. We evaluate at calibrated operating point: fix the global FMR to target α {1%, 0.1%} via τα = Quantileα ({Di : yi=0}), then measure per-group FNMR. This reflects realistic deployment where an operator fixes tolerable false-alarm rate. To normalize for absolute model quality and isolate relative group (dis)advantage, we adopt the Skewed Error Ratio (SER), inspired by [31]: SERg(α) = FNMRg(α) FNMRglobal(α) . (2) Unlike the original formulation - which takes the ratio of worst to best group we anchor to the global population FNMR, avoiding division-by-zero when any group achieves perfect recall and decoupling group disadvantage from the best groups advantage. SER = 1.0 is perfect parity; SER > 1 indicates disproportionate miss burden. We report SERmax = maxg SERg (lower = fairer).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced SynthFaces, large-scale, identity-grouped and captioned synthetic human dataset designed for demographic balance while reducing reliance on released images of real individuals. Its ID-Flow sampler provides explicit demographic control while maintaining identity diversity and empirical separation from the real identities used for training. Across personalized generation, face recognition, and demographic VQA, models trained with SynthFaces improve subgroup parity while retaining useful task performance. These results show that controlling identity composition during dataset construction is an effective lever for fairer human-centric models. Future work should reduce dependence on potentially biased face encoders and foundation generators and investigate hybrid realsynthetic balancing strategies.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: KARPUKHIN ET AL.: SYNTHFACES While SynthFaces addresses key gaps in existing datasets, several limitations should be acknowledged. Bias inheritance from foundation models. Arc2Face and Flux despite being state of the art generators for corresponding parts of pipeline carry aesthetic and demographic biases from their respective training corpora. Our pipeline guarantees label-level balance across age, race, and gender, but within-group visual diversity and image style remain bounded by what these upstream models can faithfully generate. Demographic combinations that are underrepresented in Arc2Faces training data may yield lower-fidelity or less varied outputs. Synthetic-to-real distribution gap. Images produced by diffusion models may contain subtle distributional artifacts absent from real photographs. While our VLM-based filtering step removes overt defects, residual domain differences could limit transferability when SynthFaces-trained models are evaluated on real-world data. Dependency on upstream model capabilities. The expressive range of generated identities is ultimately constrained by Arc2Faces capacity for identity preservation and Fluxs generation quality. Improvements to either foundation model would directly benefit downstream dataset quality, but also introduce moving dependency.

sections.title: 8 Ethics statement
sections.content: The creation of SynthFaces is direct response to the ethical crisis surrounding web-scraped human-centric datasets, many of which have been rightfully retracted due to non-consensual use of personal images, including those of minors. To reduce these privacy and consent risks, SynthFaces releases synthetic identities generated by our pipeline rather than scraped personal images. Because ID-Flow is trained from ArcFace embeddings extracted from real datasets, we do not claim formal privacy guarantee; instead, we empirically evaluate nearest-neighbor separation with the ID-NonLeak metric and design the dataset to avoid direct re-use of real personal images. Furthermore, we address the issue of demographic bias that plagues both real and synthetic datasets. Our pipeline is explicitly designed to generate balanced representation across age, gender, and ethnicity, creating resource purposed for training fairer models and mitigating the harmful disparities common in existing technologies. While we acknowledge that no synthetic data is perfect and subtle biases may persist, we believe this work demonstrates responsible path forward, decoupling progress in human-centric computer vision from the exploitation of personal data.

For the sphere, integration can be performed by projecting updates onto the tangent space and mapping back via the exponential map at each step. A.3 Additional data and model details Data collection Our training stage is conducted fully in latent space of ArcFace embedding. To obtain them, we first processed images from Cosmic-HQ, FFHQ, EasyPortait and also enriched with images of people from the internet. We included only embeddings that were detectable with fixed bounding box size set to 640, since embeddings tend to significantly differ depending on detection size. We implement deduplication stage, where all collected embeddings are filtered out by threshold value of 0.4 pairwise cosine similarity, ensuring diverse faces are used for training and avoiding identity collapse, where model learns only fixed amount of identities. Then we also annotate all collected images with FairFace, providing age/race/gender labels, and remove embeddings that correspond to images that failed labeling stage. As result, we train on around 50k identity embeddings with labels. For evaluation we use hold-out set of Cosmic-HQ images and CelebA, which werent used during training, and apply same pipeline to obtain embeddings and labels, without deduplication stage. A.4 Similarity filtering of identities Figure 11: Examples removed by image-statistics filtering. Low entropy corresponds to heavily stylized samples; low saturation identifies grayscale images, while high saturation exposes unnatural colors and lighting artifacts. In order to measure diversity of embeddings themselves, we analyzed distribution of pairwise distance to closest neighbor within data itself. It can be seen in Figure 12 these distributions before and after filtering images based of this metric thresholding - tails of labels that under-perform are dropped, sacrificing ideal uniform distribution of labels for better face diversity. Comparison of diversity metrics to compare before and after are given in Table 13. The reason for such difference in diversity performance is expected due to inherit bias of underlying training data - even after filtering, certain categories remain unrepresented, which hurts model variability. We modify collected captions by ensuring trigger-word is added single time next to person descriptor. We finetune LoRA modules attached to linear layers in attention blocks with rank=16 with Adam-W optimizer, learning rate set to 1e 5, use linear warm up for approximately 2k iterations and train in total for 20000 iterations with bs=4.
